title: The harm of slander
hook: slandering the holy spoils the slanderer's own life (Sukhmani 13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salok of ashtpadi 13, sant, and your line: honor the good. Did you tell one good person what you admire in them? Today the salok's second line takes over the whole ashtpadi. Day four hundred eighty-seven.

A group chat, late at night. Someone posts a screenshot of a coworker's message and adds an eye-roll. Within a minute there are six replies. Everyone has a story. Nobody is lying exactly, but by the end the coworker is a joke, and the chat has never been livelier. It feels good, in a sour sort of way. You go to sleep a little buzzed and a little worse. Guru Arjan spends an entire ashtpadi on that buzz, and he keeps asking one question that the group chat never does: what is this doing to us?
screen: `A SCREENSHOT AND AN EYE-ROLL.` → `SIX REPLIES IN A MINUTE.` → `WHAT IS THIS DOING TO US?`

segments.voice: The thirteenth ashtpadi is built like a drumbeat. Line after line begins with the same three words: sant kai dookhan. Through harming the holy, through speaking ill of them. And then each line names a cost. Through slandering the holy, the text says, life is cut short. Through slandering the holy, all peace goes. The mind becomes dirty. Honor is lost. No one comes to help. The list keeps going, stanza after stanza, the same opening words returning like a knock on a door. Now look at who pays in every single line. Not the sant. The good person being slandered is never the one who suffers in these stanzas. The losses all fall on the slanderer: their peace, their mind, their standing, their life. That's the surprise in this ashtpadi, and it turns the group chat upside down. We gossip because it seems to cost the other person something and give us something: a laugh, a bond, a bit of height. Sukhmani says the accounts run the other way. The one being talked about loses very little. The one talking is the one being emptied. Two words are worth holding. Dookhan: speaking ill, finding fault, doing harm with words. And nindaa, slander, the word the salok itself uses. Even so, the first stanza ends with a door left open: if the merciful saint shows mercy, even the slanderer is carried across in the saints' company. And why the holy, especially? Because, as yesterday's salok said, nearness to the good lifts us. Slander is the opposite of nearness. It pushes the good away from us on purpose, and with them, the very company that might have carried us across.
screen: `SANT KAI DOOKHAN: A DRUMBEAT.` · `LINE AFTER LINE, A COST.` · `THE SLANDERER ALWAYS PAYS.` · `PUSHING THE GOOD AWAY.` · then, large: `SLANDER HARMS THE SLANDERER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say nothing unkind, even inside. For these two minutes, sit and let the mind do what it does. It will probably bring up someone who annoys you and start a little commentary. When it does, don't argue with it. Just stop the sentence halfway, like lifting a needle off a record. Breathe out. Wait for the next one. You're not forcing kindness yet; you're only learning where the needle is. The bell holds the time.
Nindaa, slander. Sant kai dookhan, speaking ill of the good: in the thirteenth ashtpadi, line after line, the one who speaks is the one who pays.
Your line: slander harms the slanderer. Today, say nothing unkind about anyone who isn't in the room. If a conversation turns that way, let your reply be silence. Day four hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib move through the thirteenth ashtpadi's repeated lines beginning sant kai dookhan, and nindaa, slander, is warned against in many hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib.

fork.setup: the group chat is roasting a kind coworker. by the thirteenth ashtpadi, who loses the most?
fork.reveal: line after line, Sukhmani says the slanderer pays: their peace, their mind, their honor. the good person loses very little.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nindaa, slander, speaking ill of someone; the word used in the salok.

trapdoor: what you thought: slander hurts the person it's about.
what it means: in Sukhmani, slander mostly hurts the one who speaks it.
what a scholar hears: the ashtpadi works by anaphora, the refrain sant kai dookhan opening line after line, each closing on a loss to the slanderer.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 13, stanzas 1–3 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279–280)

notes: Paraphrased costs in the sant kai dookhan lines (aarjaa ghatai: life shortened; sukh sabh jaai: peace lost; mat hoi maleen: mind made dirty; sobhaa te heen: honor lost; no one to help): confirm each appears in ashtpadi 13 and their stanza numbers.
Dookhan glossed as speaking ill / harming, related to dookh: confirm the gloss.
Some lines of the ashtpadi also speak of the saint's slanderer in narak, hell; the script paraphrases only the costs listed.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'dookhan, from dookh, pain' (dookhan is usually traced to Sanskrit dushan, defiling or fault-finding, not dukh, pain: a preacher's etymology) and the superlative 'the most common word in Gurbani'; added the end of stanza 1 (sant kirpaal kirpaa je karai, Nanak santsang nindak bhee tarai) so the ashtpadi isn't shown as only threats.
